setting: A civil trial concerns a broken display window. The witness was in a different town and learned nothing through any admissible source; counsel asks for her own account of the impact.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What struck the window that night?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I wasn't there. I suppose it was a thrown stone.

explanation: The witness has no firsthand basis for describing what struck the window.
trap_note: A plausible guess does not supply personal knowledge.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a missing safe. The witness was asleep throughout the removal and did not see anyone enter the building.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Who carried the safe out?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I couldn't see anything; I was asleep upstairs.

explanation: The witness cannot identify a person she did not perceive.
trap_note: Being in the building does not establish knowledge of everything that happened there.

setting: A civil trial concerns a damaged boat engine. The witness never opened the engine or watched anyone inspect it and has no technical expertise.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Which internal part had snapped?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I don't know. I've never seen the inside of it.

explanation: The witness lacks a firsthand basis for identifying the internal damage.
trap_note: Owning a boat does not establish personal knowledge of unseen engine parts.

setting: A civil trial concerns a disputed delivery. The receptionist left before the courier arrived and never saw the parcel.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Was the parcel already torn when it arrived?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I had gone home by then, so I didn't see it.

explanation: The witness did not observe the parcel's arrival or condition.
trap_note: Working at the delivery address does not supply knowledge of an event missed.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a cash-box theft. A witness could see only the closed shop door and not the room where the box was kept.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What was happening inside the office?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I couldn't see inside. The door was shut.

explanation: The witness cannot describe unseen events inside the office.
trap_note: A nearby vantage point is insufficient when it provides no view of the event.

setting: A civil trial concerns a loose roof panel. The witness never visited the roof and is asked whether a particular screw was missing.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Was the corner screw in place that morning?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I never went up there, so I couldn't tell you.

explanation: There is no personal observation supporting the proposed testimony about the screw.
trap_note: Familiarity with the building does not establish knowledge of its unseen roof hardware.

setting: A civil trial concerns a damaged parcel. The witness saw the unopened box but never saw its contents before delivery.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Was the vase cracked before it was packed?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I only saw the sealed box. I didn't see the vase.

explanation: Seeing the sealed package does not establish knowledge of the vase's earlier condition.
trap_note: Observation of a container is not observation of its contents.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a disputed telephone call. The witness was not present, did not hear the call, and has no recording.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What words did the caller use?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I didn't hear the call myself.

explanation: The witness lacks a firsthand basis for recounting words she never heard.
trap_note: Knowing the participants does not supply knowledge of their conversation.

setting: A civil trial concerns a driver's view at a junction. The witness was facing away when the vehicles approached.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Which signal was showing as the van entered?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: My back was to the lights then.

explanation: The witness did not perceive the signal at the relevant time.
trap_note: Knowing the junction's layout does not establish which light was showing.

setting: A civil trial concerns disputed damage to a rented violin. The witness first saw it after the rental ended and is asked about its earlier condition.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Was that crack there before the rental began?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I didn't see the violin until it came back.

explanation: The witness's later observation cannot establish the earlier condition without another proper basis.
trap_note: Personal knowledge of one time does not automatically extend to another.

setting: A criminal trial concerns an alleged threatening email. Counsel offers a printout found on a public bench, and nobody can identify its sender, account, or origin.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: How do you know this email came from the defendant?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I don't. I just found the printout outside.

explanation: No evidence connects the printout to the defendant as claimed.
trap_note: Readable text does not by itself authenticate its purported author.

setting: A civil trial concerns a disputed photograph of a damaged fence. The witness has never visited the location and knows nothing about the photograph's source.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Does this accurately show the fence involved in this case?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I couldn't say. I've never seen that fence.

explanation: The offered photograph lacks evidence that it depicts the claimed fence.
trap_note: A photograph need not be authenticated by its photographer, but some adequate identifying basis is required.

setting: A criminal trial concerns an alleged recorded confession. The recording's origin is unknown, and the witness does not recognize the voice.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Whose voice is on this recording?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I don't recognize it, and I don't know where the file came from.

explanation: Nothing establishes that the recording contains the defendant's voice as claimed.
trap_note: The words on a recording do not alone prove who spoke them.

setting: A civil trial concerns a disputed text agreement. The witness offers an unexplained screenshot without knowing either number or having any identifying context.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: How do you connect this screenshot to the seller?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I can't. Someone left it on my desk.

explanation: The screenshot lacks evidence linking it to the seller or alleged exchange.
trap_note: Digital material needs authentication just as paper evidence does.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a knife allegedly recovered from a locker. The witness presents a similar knife but cannot identify where it came from or connect it to the search.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Is this the knife recovered from that locker?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I don't know. It was in a box with several others.

explanation: No evidence identifies this knife as the item allegedly recovered.
trap_note: Similarity alone may be insufficient when there is no identifying connection to the event.

setting: A civil trial concerns a warehouse temperature chart. The proponent cannot identify the instrument, location, or process that produced the chart.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What recorded these temperatures?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I don't know which sensor it was or where it was installed.

explanation: The proponent has not shown that the chart measures the claimed warehouse conditions.
trap_note: Numbers on a chart need a reliable connection to what they supposedly represent.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a purported online advertisement. The only witness cannot identify the webpage, seller, or date and offers an unexplained image.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Where did you obtain this image?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I can't remember. I don't know whose listing it was.

explanation: The image has not been connected to the claimed advertisement.
trap_note: An online-looking layout does not establish a document's source.

setting: A civil trial concerns the exact cancellation clause in an available signed contract. Counsel offers a witness's memory of its wording instead of the contract, with no basis for dispensing with it.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What exactly did the cancellation clause say?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I remember it said you had to give thirty days' notice.

explanation: Proving the contract's wording generally requires the original or an admissible substitute.
trap_note: A witness's accurate memory alone does not remove the rule when the writing's contents are being proved.

setting: A civil trial concerns the precise amount written on an available receipt. No loss or other exception is claimed, and counsel asks for oral proof of the receipt's text.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What amount was printed on that receipt?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: It said nine hundred and forty dollars.

explanation: The receipt or an admissible substitute is required to prove its written amount.
trap_note: The issue is the document's contents, not merely a transaction the witness independently remembers.

setting: A criminal trial concerns the exact words in an available recorded message. The prosecution offers only a listener's recollection, without any basis for dispensing with the recording.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Repeat the words on the recording.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: It said, "Leave the package behind the station."

explanation: The recording or an admissible substitute is generally needed to prove its contents.
trap_note: Hearing a recording firsthand does not automatically permit oral proof of its contents.

setting: A civil trial concerns whether an available map labels a strip as a public lane. The witness is asked to recount the label rather than offer the map or a permitted substitute.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What label appears on that strip of the map?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: It says "Public lane" in small letters.

explanation: The map's contents should be proved by the original or an admissible substitute.
trap_note: The dispute concerns what the map says, not the witness's independent observation of the land.

setting: A civil trial concerns the exact warranty period in an available brochure. The proponent offers oral recollection only and establishes no exception.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: How long did the brochure promise coverage?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: It said five years, as I remember it.

explanation: The brochure or an admissible substitute is needed to prove the written promise.
trap_note: A witness may describe independent events, but this question asks for the writing's contents.

setting: A criminal trial concerns the exact image shown in an available security video. Counsel asks a viewer to describe that image instead of offering the video, without establishing an exception.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did frame twenty-three show?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: A hand holding a folded note beside the till.

explanation: The video or an admissible substitute is generally required to prove the image it contains.
trap_note: The witness observed the video rather than the underlying event itself.

setting: A civil trial concerns the precise date typed into an available lease amendment. Counsel offers a witness's recollection instead of the document, with no exception established.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What date was typed beside the signature?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: The first of September.

explanation: The amendment or an admissible substitute is needed to establish its written date.
trap_note: The rule addresses proof of document contents even when the witness personally read them.

setting: A civil trial concerns an available recording's exact spoken price. A witness remembers listening to it but did not attend the negotiation.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What price did the recording state?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: The speaker said twelve thousand dollars.

explanation: Proof of the recording's contents calls for the recording or an admissible substitute.
trap_note: The witness has no independent account of the negotiation to offer instead.

setting: A civil trial concerns a collision beside a bakery. The witness personally saw the impact and is asked to describe it, although a video also exists.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did you see when the van turned?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Its rear corner caught the parked bicycle and knocked it onto the pavement.

explanation: The witness may describe an event personally observed without producing a video of it.
trap_note: The best-evidence rule applies to proving a recording's contents, not every event that happened to be recorded.

setting: A civil trial concerns a photographed crack in a wall. The tenant recognizes the room and confirms the photograph accurately depicts what she saw.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Does this picture fairly show the wall that morning?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Yes. That's the crack beside my kitchen window, just as I saw it.

explanation: A witness with knowledge can authenticate a photograph as an accurate depiction.
trap_note: The authenticating witness need not have taken the photograph.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a recorded voice. A longtime colleague recognizes the speaker from years of ordinary conversation, and no other objection is at issue.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: How do you recognize that voice?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I've worked beside Imani for six years. That's how she sounds every day.

explanation: Familiarity acquired through ordinary conversation can support identification of a recorded voice.
trap_note: Voice identification does not always require a forensic expert.

setting: A civil trial concerns the contents of a signed agreement. An accurate photocopy is offered, with no genuine authenticity dispute or unfairness in using it.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Is this a complete copy of the signed agreement?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Yes. I copied every page directly from the signed original.

explanation: An accurate duplicate is ordinarily admissible unless authenticity or fairness creates a genuine issue.
trap_note: The best-evidence rule does not categorically require the one physical original.

setting: A civil trial concerns a missing receipt destroyed accidentally in a house fire. The proponent did not act in bad faith, and an eyewitness recalls the receipt's contents.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What amount did you see on the receipt before the fire?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: It showed a payment of two hundred dollars.

explanation: Other evidence of contents is permitted when originals are destroyed without bad faith.
trap_note: The original-writing requirement has an exception for innocent loss or destruction.

setting: A civil trial concerns a cashier's actions. The witness stood beside the till and describes what she personally observed.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did you see the cashier do with the envelope?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: She opened it, counted the notes, and put them in the drawer.

explanation: The witness has a direct observational basis for describing the cashier's conduct.
trap_note: A witness does not need an expert qualification to describe an ordinary event personally seen.
